data.text: I have comprehensive coverage of all five 2026 meetings. Let me submit my findings.

data.answer: Across the five 2026 FOMC meetings, participants' labor-market assessment evolved from "stabilizing after gradual cooling" (January) through a period of debate about softening (March–April) to a clear view of a stable, balanced, and modestly strengthening market (June–July). In January, the unemployment rate was 4.4% (Dec) and job gains were low, with most participants seeing stabilization after a period of gradual cooling; layoffs and hiring were both low, and business contacts were cautious about hiring amid economic uncertainty and AI/automation concerns [D29][D30]. By March, the unemployment rate was still 4.4% (Feb) and job gains low (partly held down by a health-care strike and harsh winter weather); most saw the market broadly in balance, but several flagged signs of potential softening (rising prime-age unemployment, job growth concentrated in health care, declining job-availability surveys), and the vast majority judged employment risks skewed to the downside, with the market "vulnerable to adverse shocks" [D32][D59][D60]. In April, the view was similar—stabilization, low job gains roughly commensurate with slow labor-force growth, though a few saw fragility, and most still judged employment risks tilted to the downside [D36][D62]. By June, the tone shifted clearly: the unemployment rate had remained stable near its longer-run level, payroll gains had strengthened and were consistent with labor-force growth, and indicators pointed to a balanced market; several noted their earlier concerns about deterioration had eased, though the job-finding rate and job-availability measures still reflected low dynamism [D39][D53][D54]. In July, participants assessed the market as stable with labor demand and supply in balance, noting payroll gains had strengthened, broadened beyond health care, and that the market had "strengthened modestly"; a few noted lingering softness (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment), and AI was seen as keeping both hiring and firing low [D41][D42][D50]. On wages: AHE rose 3.8% y/y in Dec 2025 and Feb 2026 (slightly below year-earlier pace), and the ECI was up 3.4% [D29][D32]; by June, nominal wage growth was seen as moderate and consistent with inflation moving toward 2%, and by July AHE was 3.5% y/y (0.4pp lower than a year earlier), with wage growth moderate overall but notable increases for skilled workers in AI-related sectors [D41][D50][D51].
key_facts: Jan 2026: Unemployment 4.4% in Dec, unchanged from Sep; average monthly payrolls turned negative in Q4 (government roll-off after deferred resignation program); AHE +3.8% y/y. Participants: job gains low, market 'stabilizing after a period of gradual cooling'; layoffs and hiring both low; business contacts cautious on hiring due to uncertainty and AI/automation [D29][D30].

Mar 2026: Unemployment 4.4% in Feb (same as Sep 2025); payroll gains low in Jan-Feb, held down by health-care strike and harsh winter weather; ECI +3.4%, AHE +3.8% y/y. Most saw market broadly in balance; several flagged softening (prime-age unemployment up, job growth concentrated in health care, declining job-availability surveys); vast majority judged employment risks skewed to the downside, market 'vulnerable to adverse shocks' [D32][D59][D60].

Apr 2026: Unemployment little changed, job gains low on average; most judged stabilization; several said low job growth was commensurate with slow labor-force growth, a few saw fragility; signs of softness included sector concentration, declining job-availability surveys, and modest wage growth; most judged employment risks tilted to the downside [D36][D62].

Jun 2026: Unemployment stable over the past year near longer-run level; payroll gains strengthened this year, consistent with labor-force growth; job openings, initial claims, layoffs stable, pointing to a balanced market; declines in job-finding rate and job-availability measures reflected low dynamism; many said earlier concerns about deterioration had eased; nominal wage growth consistent with inflation moving toward 2% [D39][D53][D54].

Jul 2026: Unemployment 4.2% in June, little changed over two years; payroll growth slowed in June but H1 average gains well above 2025 pace; AHE +3.5% y/y (0.4pp below year earlier). Participants: market stable, demand and supply in balance; payroll gains strengthened and broadened beyond health care; market 'strengthened modestly'; a few noted lingering softness (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment); AI keeping hiring and firing low; wage growth moderate, with notable increases for skilled AI-sector workers (electricians, machinists, engineers) [D41][D42][D50][D51].

Evolution: Jan 'stabilizing after gradual cooling' → Mar/Apr debate over softening with downside-skewed employment risks → Jun/Jul stable, balanced, modestly strengthening market with eased concerns. Policy: rates held at 3.5-3.75% at all five meetings; easing-bias language removed from the statement by June [D31][D37][D55].

Powell (Jan 28): conditions "may be stabilizing after a period of gradual softening"; unemployment 4.4% (December), job gains low, total nonfarm payrolls down 22,000/month over the prior three months (private payrolls +29,000/month); openings, layoffs, hiring and nominal wage growth "show little change"; in Q&A he cited a very low Conference Board job-availability reading and a significant rise in part-time-for-economic-reasons as "little places that suggest the labor market has softened" [D12][D13][D67][D68]. Powell (Apr 29, his last as Chair): unemployment 4.3% (March), "little changed"; job gains low; other indicators "generally show little change"; in Q&A he called 4.3% "a low rate... close to mainstream estimates of the natural rate" but described "an unusual and uncomfortable kind of a balance" with quits and hires "really low" and "effectively no new net job creation" [D17][D19][D73]. data.text: I now have comprehensive coverage of the MPR and the 2026 Governor speeches on the labor market. Let me submit my findings.

data.answer:
Across the July 2026 Monetary Policy Report and the 2026 speeches by Governors, the dominant labor-market story is a transition from a fragile, weakening market in late 2025 to a stabilized, roughly balanced "low-hire, low-fire" market in 2026, with the unemployment rate holding near its estimated natural rate (~4.1-4.4%) and the balance of policy risks shifting from employment toward inflation.

The MPR (2026-07-10) concludes the labor market "has stabilized, with demand and supply roughly in balance": the unemployment rate was 4.2% in June, low and little changed since last summer; layoffs subdued; job vacancies roughly flat; and private payroll gains picking up from ~30,000/month in H2 2025 to ~80,000 in Q1 and ~100,000 in Q2 2026, though still soft by historical standards. It attributes the low job-creation need to historically low labor-supply growth (aging population plus a sharp drop in net immigration), and Box 1 notes employment disparities remain narrow but real wage gains for some disadvantaged groups have moderated.

Waller's views evolved most clearly: in "Labor Market Data: Signal or Noise?" (2026-02-23) he called 2025 the weakest job-creation year outside a recession since 2002 (payrolls probably fell), treated the strong January report as possibly noise, and kept the balance of risks tilted toward easing. By "One Transitory Shock After Another" (2026-04-17) he still saw a vulnerable market (low hires and low fires, employers "walking a tightrope"). In "Policy Risks Have Changed" (2026-05-22) he judged supply and demand finally in rough balance (April unemployment 4.3%, near his long-run estimate) and said a weakening labor market was no longer the dominant policy force—his focus shifted to inflation, supporting removal of the "easing bias." By "Monetary Policy at a Crossroads" (2026-07-13) and the Reuters interview (2026-09-03) he described the market as stable and balanced, "in satisfactory shape," with job creation averaging ~60,000/month through July and unemployment at 4.1%, and said his focus would be on inflation.

Other Governors tracked the same arc. Bowman was the most bearish early on: in January 2026 she called the market "increasingly fragile," with private job gains of only ~30,000/month in Q4 2025 and the Conference Board job-availability index at its lowest since early 2021. Jefferson (Jan 16, Mar 26, Apr 7, Oct 1) moved from "downside risks to employment appear to have risen" (Jan) to "roughly in balance" with the unemployment rate near its natural rate (Apr) to "conditions have stabilized," with the rate ticking down to 4.1% in August and payroll gains broadening (Oct). Cook (Feb 4, Jul 15, Aug 5) consistently described a market "roughly in balance"/stable, noting the low-hire, low-fire environment hits new entrants hardest and that risks had shifted toward inflation. Barr (Feb 17) framed the current market as a "delicate balance" and focused on AI's potential labor-market effects (early-career workers in AI-exposed occupations already seeing employment declines).

Overall, 2026 saw a consensus shift from concern about labor-market deterioration (early 2026) to confidence in stabilization (mid-to-late 2026), with the policy debate centering on inflation rather than employment.
key_facts: MPR July 2026 Summary: 'Following a period of cooling, the labor market has stabilized, with demand and supply roughly in balance. The unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent in June, was low and has been little changed since last summer.' [D164]

Taking "over 2026" to mean the full calendar year, using the five 2026 FOMC meetings (Jan 28, Mar 18, Apr 29, Jun 17, Jul 29) and 2026-dated documents: the Federal Reserve's view of the labor market shifted from a fragile, softening market in early 2026 to a stable, balanced, and modestly strengthening one by mid-to-late 2026. The unemployment rate held near its estimated natural rate throughout, but the characterization of job growth moved from "remained low" to "kept pace with the workforce," and the balance of policy risks tilted from employment toward inflation. (A sixth 2026 statement dated September 16, 2026 exists in the collection but falls outside the five meetings covered here.)

## The arc in one line
- **Jan–Apr 2026 (Chair Powell):** "stabilizing after a period of gradual softening/cooling"; job gains "remained low"; employment risks skewed to the downside; the market "vulnerable to adverse shocks."
- **Jun–Jul 2026 (Chair Warsh):** "stable," "balanced," "strengthened modestly"; job gains "kept pace with the workforce"; earlier concerns about deterioration had eased; the labor market "not currently a source of inflationary pressures."

## FOMC statement wording, meeting by meeting
The single labor-market sentence in each statement shows the clearest change in tone:

| Meeting | Statement language on the labor market |
|---|---|
| Jan 28, 2026 | "Job gains have remained low, and the unemployment rate has shown some signs of stabilization." [D56] |
| Mar 18, 2026 | "Job gains have remained low, and the unemployment rate has been little changed in recent months." [D57] |
| Apr 29, 2026 | "Job gains have remained low, on average, and the unemployment rate has been little changed in recent months." [D58] |
| Jun 17, 2026 | "Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little." [D48] |
| Jul 29, 2026 | "Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little." [D49] |

Key shifts: (1) job-gains language upgraded from "remained low" (Jan–Apr) to "kept pace with the workforce" (Jun–Jul), with an "on average" qualifier added only in April; (2) unemployment phrasing moved from "shown some signs of stabilization" (Jan) to "little changed in recent months" (Mar, Apr) to "changed little" (Jun, Jul); (3) no 2026 statement mentioned wage growth; (4) the June and July statements added "Productivity growth and capital investment are strong" and dropped the "Available/Recent indicators suggest" framing, and the two labor sentences were identical. [D56][D57][D58][D48][D49]

## What participants said in the minutes
- **Jan 28, 2026:** Unemployment 4.4% in December (unchanged from September); average monthly payrolls turned negative in Q4 (government roll-off after the deferred resignation program); AHE +3.8% y/y. Most saw the market "stabilizing after a period of gradual cooling," with both layoffs and hiring low; business contacts were cautious on hiring amid uncertainty and AI/automation concerns. [D29][D30]
- **Mar 18, 2026:** Unemployment 4.4% in February; payroll gains low (held down by a health-care strike and harsh winter weather); ECI +3.4%, AHE +3.8% y/y. Most saw the market broadly in balance, but several flagged softening (rising prime-age unemployment, job growth concentrated in health care, declining job-availability surveys); the vast majority judged employment risks skewed to the downside and the market "vulnerable to adverse shocks." [D32][D59][D60]
- **Apr 29, 2026:** Unemployment little changed; job gains low on average; most judged stabilization, with several noting low job growth was commensurate with slow labor-force growth, though a few saw fragility; most still judged employment risks tilted to the downside. [D36][D62]
- **Jun 17, 2026:** Unemployment stable near its longer-run level; payroll gains strengthened and were consistent with labor-force growth; job openings, claims, and layoffs stable, pointing to a balanced market; many said earlier concerns about deterioration had eased, though the job-finding rate and job-availability measures still reflected low dynamism; nominal wage growth consistent with inflation moving toward 2%. [D39][D53][D54]
- **Jul 29, 2026:** Unemployment 4.2% in June, little changed over two years; H1 average payroll gains well above the 2025 pace; AHE +3.5% y/y (0.4pp below a year earlier). Participants saw the market stable with demand and supply in balance, payroll gains broadened beyond health care, and the market "strengthened modestly"; a few noted lingering softness (low job-finding rate, elevated long-term unemployment); AI was seen as keeping both hiring and firing low. [D41][D42]

## The Chair's characterization
Note that Jerome Powell chaired the January, March, and April 2026 meetings; Kevin Warsh became Chair in June 2026, so the June and July press conferences and the July 14 testimony are Warsh's.

- **Powell, Jan 28:** conditions "may be stabilizing after a period of gradual softening"; unemployment 4.4% (December); total nonfarm payrolls −22,000/month over the prior three months (private +29,000/month); in Q&A he cited a very low Conference Board job-availability reading and a significant rise in part-time-for-economic-reasons as "little places that suggest the labor market has softened." [D12][D13][D67][D68]
- **Powell, Mar 18:** unemployment 4.4% (February), "little changed since late last summer"; job gains low; SEP median unemployment 4.4% this year; in Q&A, "the labor market is clearly not a source of inflationary pressures." [D14][D70][D155]
- **Powell, Apr 29 (his last as Chair):** unemployment 4.3% (March), "little changed"; in Q&A he called 4.3% "a low rate… close to mainstream estimates of the natural rate" but described "an unusual and uncomfortable kind of a balance" with quits and hires "really low" and "effectively no new net job creation." [D17][D19][D73]
- **Warsh, Jun 17 (first meeting):** "Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little"; SEP unemployment ~4.3%; in Q&A the Committee "thought that the labor markets were stable," some saw it "trending better than that," "the jobs data's been moving in a good direction," and strong productivity-led growth is "something we embrace." [D20][D22][D76]
- **Warsh, Jul 29:** same statement language; in Q&A "labor markets—solid, steady," and he rejected a tradeoff, saying delivering price stability will also deliver full employment. [D23][D25][D79][D154]
- **Warsh, Jul 14 testimony:** "America's labor market appears broadly stable. Job creation has kept pace with the workforce. The unemployment rate is low and has changed little over the past year. We're seeing relatively few layoffs, only slight variance in the rate of job vacancies, and solid growth in nominal wages." [D112]

However, it omits or under-covers several key reference facts: it does not state the September 2026 FOMC statement’s labor-market language, does not give the SEP median 2026 unemployment projection as lowered from 4.4% in March to 4.1% in September, and does not attribute the ~4.1% August unemployment figure to Warsh.
